examples.question_text:
Two fair coins are tossed independently. Two heads wins $\$8$, exactly one head wins $\$2$, and no heads loses $\$4$.
Let $X$ be the return in dollars. Construct its probability distribution and calculate the expected return.
examples.solution_text:
The four equally likely outcomes are $HH$, $HT$, $TH$ and $TT$.

$\begin{array}{c|ccc}x&-4&2&8\\\hline P(X=x)&\frac14&\frac12&\frac14\\xP(X=x)&-1&1&2\end{array}$

$\begin{aligned}E(X)&=\sum xP(X=x)\\&=-1+1+2\\&=2\end{aligned}$

The expected return is $\$2$ per play.

examples.question_text:
A game costs $\$4$ to play. It pays $\$18$ with probability $0.1$, $\$6$ with probability $0.2$, and nothing otherwise.
Find the expected net gain, decide whom the game favours, and find the entry fee that would make it fair.
examples.solution_text:
Let $X$ be the net gain in dollars from one play. The remaining probability is $1-0.1-0.2=0.7$.

$\begin{array}{c|ccc}x&-4&2&14\\\hline P(X=x)&0.7&0.2&0.1\\xP(X=x)&-2.8&0.4&1.4\end{array}$

$\begin{aligned}E(X)&=-2.8+0.4+1.4\\&=-1\end{aligned}$

The player loses $\$1$ per play on average, so the game favours the operator.

Let $R$ be the prize in dollars.

$\begin{aligned}E(R)&=0(0.7)+6(0.2)+18(0.1)\\&=3\end{aligned}$

A fair entry fee equals the expected prize, so it is $\$3$.

examples.question_text: A stall's game has an expected net gain to the player of $-\$0.60$ per play. Find the stall's expected profit from $350$ plays. Is this profit guaranteed?
examples.solution_text:
The stall gains $\$0.60$ per play on average.

$\begin{aligned}E(\text{total profit})&=350(0.60)\\&=210\end{aligned}$

The expected profit is $\$210$. This is an average; the actual profit from $350$ plays can be higher or lower.

examples.question_text:
Game A gives a net gain of $\$7$ with probability $0.3$ and a net loss of $\$3$ otherwise. Game B gives a net gain of $\$4$ with probability $0.6$ and a net loss of $\$5$ otherwise.
Which game should a player choose based on expected net gain?
examples.solution_text:
Let $A$ and $B$ be the net gains in dollars from the respective games.

$\begin{aligned}E(A)&=7(0.3)+(-3)(0.7)\\&=2.1-2.1\\&=0\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}E(B)&=4(0.6)+(-5)(0.4)\\&=2.4-2\\&=0.4\end{aligned}$

Choose Game B: its expected net gain is $\$0.40$ per play, compared with $\$0$ for Game A.

examples.question_text:
A bag contains $10$ counters: $5$ red, $3$ blue and $2$ gold. One counter is drawn at random. The respective prizes are $\$k$, $\$2k$ and $\$4k$.
Find the exact value of $k$ that makes an entry fee of $\$8$ fair. Give its approximation to two decimal places.
examples.solution_text:
Let $R$ be the prize in dollars.

$\begin{aligned}E(R)&=k\left(\frac5{10}\right)+2k\left(\frac3{10}\right)+4k\left(\frac2{10}\right)\\&=\frac{19k}{10}\end{aligned}$

For a fair game, the expected prize equals the entry fee.

$\begin{aligned}\frac{19k}{10}&=8\\19k&=80\\k&=\frac{80}{19}\\&\approx4.21\end{aligned}$

The exact fair value is $k=\frac{80}{19}$, approximately $\$4.21$. Using the rounded value gives only an approximately fair game.

examples.question_text:
An insurer charges a $\$120$ premium and keeps it whether or not a claim is made. With probability $0.04$, it pays a claim of $\$1000$; otherwise it pays nothing.
Let $X$ be the insurer's profit in dollars on one policy. Find the expected profit, variance and standard deviation, rounding the standard deviation to two decimal places.
examples.solution_text:
A claim gives a profit of $120-1000=-880$ dollars. No claim gives a profit of $120$ dollars.

$\begin{array}{c|cc}x&-880&120\\\hline P(X=x)&0.04&0.96\\xP(X=x)&-35.2&115.2\\x^2P(X=x)&30\,976&13\,824\end{array}$

$\begin{aligned}\mu=E(X)&=-35.2+115.2\\&=80\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}E(X^2)&=30\,976+13\,824\\&=44\,800\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}\mathrm{Var}(X)&=E(X^2)-\mu^2\\&=44\,800-80^2\\&=38\,400\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}\sigma&=\sqrt{38\,400}\\&\approx195.96\end{aligned}$

The expected profit is $\$80$, the variance is $38\,400$ dollars squared, and the standard deviation is approximately $\$195.96$.

coverage.summary: Authored six worked examples covering all distinct accepted assessment methods, including an unknown fair-prize parameter. Assessments were classified only; their mathematics was neither changed nor re-audited. New working was checked against the supplied teaching methods and independently recalculated. Separate editable prompts and solutions use single-dollar mathematics, relation-aligned working and automatic solution colouring. No diagrams are needed for these tabular monetary methods. No files were written; independent review and actual rendering verification remain later stages.

examples.derivation: HH, HT, TH and TT give returns 8, 2, 2 and -4. Their grouped probabilities are 1/4, 1/2 and 1/4. E(X)=-4/4+2/2+8/4=2 dollars. This adapts Mixed Applications Foundation Q1 using the taught product-row method.

The zero-prize probability is 0.7. Net gains -4, 2 and 14 have weighted products -2.8, 0.4 and 1.4, giving E(X)=-1 dollar. Expected prize is 6(0.2)+18(0.1)=3 dollars, so the operator is favoured and the fair fee is 3 dollars. The source teaches both net-gain judgement and fair-fee calculation.
Operator expected profit is 0.60 dollars per play; 350(0.60)=210 dollars. An expected total is not guaranteed. This follows the operator-profit calculation in Mixed Applications Foundation Q2.

E(A)=7(0.3)-3(0.7)=0 dollars. E(B)=4(0.6)-5(0.4)=0.40 dollars. Game B has the greater expected net gain. The source's comparison of expected values supports this method, with monetary interpretation supplied by its games-of-chance teaching.

Expected prize is (5k+6k+8k)/10=19k/10. Fairness requires 19k/10=8, giving k=80/19, approximately 4.21 dollars. The rounded parameter yields only approximate fairness. This directly adapts the unknown-prize method in Mixed Applications Mastery Q15.

Profits are -880 and 120 with probabilities 0.04 and 0.96. E(X)=-35.2+115.2=80 dollars. E(X²)=774400(0.04)+14400(0.96)=30976+13824=44800. Variance is 44800-6400=38400 dollars squared; standard deviation is sqrt(38400), approximately 195.96 dollars. This follows the source's first-moment, second-moment and square-root method.
